content.prompt: An investment of $\$200\,000$ made on the 2nd of January is earning $\$823$ per month in simple interest. The interest is paid into the account on the 1st of each month. Count January of the investment year as month 1; the first interest payment is on 1 February.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down an equation for the balance $B$ of the account on the 1st of the $n$th month.

answer.worked:
On 1 February, $n=2$ and one interest payment has been made. On the first day of month $n$, there have been $n-1$ payments.
$$B=200\,000+823(n-1),\qquad n\ge2.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the last time that the total balance of the account is no more than $\$205\,000$.

answer.short: 31 July of the investment year, immediately before the 1 August interest payment.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}200\,000+823(n-1)&\le205\,000\\823(n-1)&\le5000\\n-1&\le\frac{5000}{823}=6+\frac{62}{823}\end{align*}$$
At most six payments can have been made. The sixth payment is on 1 July, when the balance is $\$204\,938$. The seventh is on 1 August, when it becomes $\$205\,761$. The last qualifying date is therefore 31 July.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the first time that the balance is greater than $\$215\,000$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}200\,000+823(n-1)&>215\,000\\823(n-1)&>15\,000\\n-1&>\frac{15\,000}{823}=18+\frac{186}{823}\end{align*}$$
The first qualifying payment count is 19. After 18 payments the balance is $\$214\,814$; after 19 it is $\$215\,637$. The nineteenth payment is on 1 August in the following year.

content.prompt: An electrical company is installing new lights in a new house. The company will charge the customer a call-out fee of $\$211$ plus $\$55$ per light. This covers both the purchase of the lights and their installation. The customer has a budget of $\$650$. What is the maximum number of lights that can be fitted?

answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the number of lights.
$$\begin{align*}211+55n&\le650\\55n&\le439\\n&\le\frac{439}{55}=7\frac{54}{55}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area of $\triangle CEF$ in terms of $x$.

answer.worked:
Subtract the three corner triangles from the square. Here $AE=L-x$ and $FB=L-x$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{CEF}&=L^2-\frac12x(L-x)-\frac12Lx-\frac12L(L-x)\\A_{CEF}&=L^2-\frac12(L^2+Lx-x^2)\\A_{CEF}&=\frac12(L^2-Lx+x^2).\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: What values may $x$ take if the area of the triangle is at most $\frac38L^2$?

answer.short:
$x=\dfrac L2$.

The completed square is non-negative, so the inequality holds only when it is zero.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\frac12(L^2-Lx+x^2)&\le\frac38L^2\\x^2-Lx+\frac14L^2&\le0\\\left(x-\frac L2\right)^2&\le0.\end{align*}$$
A square is non-negative, so equality is required. Hence $x=\frac L2$, which satisfies $0\le x\le L$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: By completing the square or otherwise, and noting the restrictions on $x$, what values does the area of $\triangle CEF$ lie between?

answer.short:
$\dfrac38L^2\le A_{CEF}\le\dfrac12L^2$.

The minimum occurs at $x=\frac L2$ and the maximum at $x=0$ or $x=L$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A_{CEF}&=\frac12(x^2-Lx+L^2)\\A_{CEF}&=\frac12\left(x-\frac L2\right)^2+\frac38L^2.\end{align*}$$
Since $0\le x\le L$, we have $0\le\left(x-\frac L2\right)^2\le\frac14L^2$. Thus
$$\frac38L^2\le A_{CEF}\le\frac12L^2.$$
The lower bound is attained at $x=\frac L2$; the upper bound is attained at $x=0$ and $x=L$.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=[-2(g+1)]^2-4(9)(1)\\\Delta&=4(g+1)^2-36\\\Delta&=4(g^2+2g-8)\end{align*}$$

(Hint: Either a graph of $\Delta$ versus $k$ or a table of test points may help.)

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=k^2-4(1)(4)\\\Delta&=k^2-16\\\Delta&=(k-4)(k+4)\end{align*}$$
Real roots require $\Delta\geq0$. The boundary values are $k=-4$ and $k=4$. At test points $k=-5,0,5$, the discriminant is respectively $9,-16,9$, so its signs on the three intervals are positive, negative, positive. Include the boundary values because equality is allowed.
$$k\leq-4\quad\text{or}\quad k\geq4.$$

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-3k)^2-4(1)(9)\\\Delta&=9k^2-36\\\Delta&=9(k-2)(k+2)\end{align*}$$
Real roots require $\Delta\geq0$. The boundary values are $k=-2$ and $k=2$. At test points $k=-3,0,3$, the discriminant is respectively $45,-36,45$, so its signs on the three intervals are positive, negative, positive. Include the boundary values because equality is allowed.
$$k\leq-2\quad\text{or}\quad k\geq2.$$

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=[-(3+k)]^2-4(1)(1)\\\Delta&=(k+3)^2-4\\\Delta&=k^2+6k+5\\\Delta&=(k+5)(k+1)\end{align*}$$
Real roots require $\Delta\geq0$. The boundary values are $k=-5$ and $k=-1$. At test points $k=-6,-3,0$, the discriminant is respectively $5,-4,5$, so its signs on the three intervals are positive, negative, positive. Include the boundary values because equality is allowed.
$$k\leq-5\quad\text{or}\quad k\geq-1.$$

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(k-2)^2-4(1)(1)\\\Delta&=k^2-4k+4-4\\\Delta&=k^2-4k\\\Delta&=k(k-4)\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
In each case, find the discriminant $\Delta$ and solve $\Delta<0$ to find any values of $\lambda$ for which the parabola has no $x$-intercepts.

(Hint: Either a graph of $\Delta$ versus $\lambda$ or a table of test points may help.)

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=\lambda^2-4(1)(1)\\\Delta&=\lambda^2-4\\\lambda^2-4&<0\\(\lambda-2)(\lambda+2)&<0\end{align*}$$
The graph of $\Delta=\lambda^2-4$ opens upwards and crosses the $\lambda$-axis at $-2$ and $2$. It is below the axis between these values.

Hence $-2<\lambda<2$.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=6^2-4\lambda(\lambda)\\\Delta&=36-4\lambda^2\\\Delta&=4(9-\lambda^2)\\4(9-\lambda^2)&<0\end{align*}$$
The graph of $\Delta=4(9-\lambda^2)$ opens downwards and crosses the $\lambda$-axis at $-3$ and $3$. It is below the axis outside these values.

Hence $\lambda<-3$ or $\lambda>3$.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(1-\lambda)^2-4(1)(-\lambda)\\\Delta&=1-2\lambda+\lambda^2+4\lambda\\\Delta&=\lambda^2+2\lambda+1\\\Delta&=(\lambda+1)^2\end{align*}$$
A square is never negative, so there are no values of $\lambda$ for which $\Delta<0$. Thus the parabola always has at least one $x$-intercept.

$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-2\lambda)^2-4\lambda[-(\lambda-2)]\\\Delta&=4\lambda^2+4\lambda(\lambda-2)\\\Delta&=8\lambda^2-8\lambda\\\Delta&=8\lambda(\lambda-1)\\8\lambda(\lambda-1)&<0\end{align*}$$
The graph of $\Delta=8\lambda(\lambda-1)$ opens upwards and crosses the $\lambda$-axis at $0$ and $1$. It is below the axis between these values.

Hence $0<\lambda<1$.

content.prompt: Questions 8 and 9 used the relationship between the discriminant and the zeroes of the quadratic $y=ax^2+bx+c$, as given in Box 4. Here you will prove those results.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Rearrange the equation of the parabola to show that
$$x^2+\frac{b}{a}x=\frac{y-c}{a},$$
then add an appropriate quantity to both sides in order to complete the square on the left hand side.

answer.worked:
Since the parabola is quadratic, $a\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}ax^2+bx&=y-c\\x^2+\frac{b}{a}x&=\frac{y-c}{a}\\x^2+\frac{b}{a}x+\frac{b^2}{4a^2}&=\frac{y-c}{a}+\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\\\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2&=\frac{y}{a}+\frac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain why there are no zeroes when $\Delta<0$. That is, explain why there is no solution if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac<0$.

answer.short: When $y=0$, $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\dfrac{\Delta}{4a^2}<0$. A real square cannot be negative, so there are no zeroes.
answer.worked:
Putting $y=0$ in part a gives
$$\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{\Delta}{4a^2}.$$
Since $4a^2>0$, the right-hand side is negative when $\Delta<0$. The left-hand side is non-negative for every real $x$, so there is no real solution.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Explain why there is a double zero when $\Delta=0$. That is, explain why there is one solution if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac=0$.

answer.short: The equation becomes $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=0$, so the single double zero is $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$.
answer.worked:
When $y=0$ and $\Delta=0$,
$$\begin{align*}\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2&=0\\x+\frac{b}{2a}&=0\\x&=-\frac{b}{2a}.\end{align*}$$
The repeated factor gives a double zero, with only one distinct value of $x$.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Explain why there are two zeroes when $\Delta>0$. That is, explain why there are two solutions if $y=0$ and $b^2-4ac>0$.

answer.short: The equation $\left(x+\dfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\dfrac{\Delta}{4a^2}>0$ has two distinct real solutions because a positive number has two square roots.
answer.worked:

content.prompt: A certain quadratic equation with rational coefficients has an irrational root. Explain why there must be a second root, and why it must be irrational.

answer.short:
There are two distinct irrational roots.

An irrational root requires a positive discriminant whose square root is irrational; both signs in the quadratic formula therefore give irrational roots.
answer.worked:
Write the equation as $ax^2+bx+c=0$, where $a,b,c$ are rational and $a\ne0$, and let $\Delta=b^2-4ac$.

The given irrational root is real, so $\Delta\ge0$. If $\Delta=0$, the only root would be $-\frac{b}{2a}$, which is rational. Thus $\Delta>0$, so there are two distinct roots:
$$x=\frac{-b+\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\quad\text{and}\quad x=\frac{-b-\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}.$$
If $\sqrt{\Delta}$ were rational, both roots would be rational, contrary to the given information. Hence $\sqrt{\Delta}$ is irrational. Adding or subtracting it from rational $-b$, then dividing by nonzero rational $2a$, gives an irrational number in each case. Therefore the second root exists and is irrational.

content.prompt: The quadratic equation $ax^2+bx+c=0$ has integer coefficients.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Suppose that the roots are rational. Explain why $4ac$ is the difference of two squares.

answer.short: The discriminant is an integer square, say $n^2$. Hence $4ac=b^2-n^2$.
answer.worked:
Rational roots require $\sqrt{\Delta}$ to be rational. Since $\Delta=b^2-4ac$ is an integer, its rational square root must be an integer. Write $\Delta=n^2$, where $n$ is an integer.
$$\begin{align*}b^2-4ac&=n^2\\4ac&=b^2-n^2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $4ac$ is the difference of the integer squares $b^2$ and $n^2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Now suppose that the roots are integers. By considering separately the sum and product of the roots, explain why both $b$ and $c$ are divisible by $a$.

answer.short: For integer roots $r,s$, $b=-a(r+s)$ and $c=ars$. Therefore $a$ divides both $b$ and $c$.
answer.worked:
Let the integer roots be $r$ and $s$. Their sum gives
$$\begin{align*}r+s&=-\frac{b}{a}\\b&=-a(r+s).\end{align*}$$
Since $r+s$ is an integer, $b$ is divisible by $a$.

Their product gives
$$\begin{align*}rs&=\frac{c}{a}\\c&=ars.\end{align*}$$
Since $rs$ is an integer, $c$ is divisible by $a$.

content.prompt: Consider the quadratic equation $\lambda x^2-(\lambda+b)x+c=0$ where both $b$ and $c$ are real numbers with $b>0$. It is known that the equation has two distinct real roots for all real values of $\lambda\ne0$. Show that $0<c<b$.

answer.short:
$0<c<b$.

The discriminant is positive for every nonzero $\lambda$; taking $\lambda=-b$ and $\lambda=b$ gives the two strict bounds.
answer.worked:
Two distinct real roots require $\Delta>0$ for every $\lambda\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(\lambda+b)^2-4\lambda c\\\Delta&=\lambda^2+2(b-2c)\lambda+b^2\\\Delta&=(\lambda+b-2c)^2+4c(b-c).\end{align*}$$
Since $b>0$, both $-b$ and $b$ are permitted nonzero values of $\lambda$.

For $\lambda=-b$:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta(-b)&=4bc>0\\c&>0.\end{align*}$$
For $\lambda=b$:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta(b)&=4b(b-c)>0\\b-c&>0\\c&<b.\end{align*}$$
Hence $0<c<b$.

content.prompt:
Let $p$, $q$ and $r$ be distinct real numbers. Substitute three appropriate values of $x$ in order to show that
$$\frac{(p-x)(q-x)}{(p-r)(q-r)}+\frac{(q-x)(r-x)}{(q-p)(r-p)}+\frac{(r-x)(p-x)}{(r-q)(p-q)}=1$$
for all values of $x$.

answer.short:
Substitute $x=p$, $x=q$ and $x=r$; the left-hand side is respectively $0+1+0$, $0+0+1$ and $1+0+0$.

The left-hand side is a polynomial of degree at most two. Agreement with $1$ at three distinct inputs proves the identity.
answer.worked:
Let $F(x)$ denote the left-hand side. Its denominators are nonzero constants because $p$, $q$ and $r$ are distinct, so write $F(x)=Ax^2+Bx+C$.

Substitute the three values:
$$\begin{align*}F(p)&=0+\frac{(q-p)(r-p)}{(q-p)(r-p)}+0=1,\\F(q)&=0+0+\frac{(r-q)(p-q)}{(r-q)(p-q)}=1,\\F(r)&=\frac{(p-r)(q-r)}{(p-r)(q-r)}+0+0=1.\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}Ap^2+Bp+C&=1,\\Aq^2+Bq+C&=1,\\Ar^2+Br+C&=1.\end{align*}$$
Subtract the second equation from the first, and the third from the second, then divide by the nonzero differences:
$$\begin{align*}A(p+q)+B&=0,\\A(q+r)+B&=0,\\A(p-r)&=0,\\A&=0,\\B&=0,\\C&=1.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $F(x)=1$ for all values of $x$.

answer.short:
$a=4(2+\sqrt2-2\sqrt3)$,

$b=-10-7\sqrt2+12\sqrt3$,

$c=3+3\sqrt2-4\sqrt3$.

Substitute the three points and solve the simultaneous equations.
answer.worked:
Substituting $P$, $Q$ and $R$ gives
$$\begin{align*}\tfrac14a+\tfrac12b+c&=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} &&(1)\\\tfrac9{16}a+\tfrac34b+c&=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} &&(2)\\a+b+c&=1 &&(3).
\end{align*}$$
Subtract (1) from (2), and (2) from (3), then multiply each result by $16$:
$$\begin{align*}5a+4b&=8\sqrt3-8\sqrt2 &&(4)\\7a+4b&=16-8\sqrt3 &&(5).
\end{align*}$$
Subtracting (4) from (5):
$$\begin{align*}2a&=16+8\sqrt2-16\sqrt3\\a&=4(2+\sqrt2-2\sqrt3).
\end{align*}$$
Using (4):
$$\begin{align*}4b&=8\sqrt3-8\sqrt2-5(8+4\sqrt2-8\sqrt3)\\4b&=-40-28\sqrt2+48\sqrt3\\b&=-10-7\sqrt2+12\sqrt3.
\end{align*}$$
Using (3):
$$\begin{align*}c&=1-(8+4\sqrt2-8\sqrt3)-(-10-7\sqrt2+12\sqrt3)\\c&=3+3\sqrt2-4\sqrt3.
\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}f(\tfrac35)&=\tfrac9{25}a+\tfrac35b+c\\f(\tfrac35)&=\tfrac9{25}(8+4\sqrt2-8\sqrt3)+\tfrac35(-10-7\sqrt2+12\sqrt3)+3+3\sqrt2-4\sqrt3\\f(\tfrac35)&=\tfrac{-3+6\sqrt2+8\sqrt3}{25}.
\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
The discriminant tells us the number of zeroes
The most obvious purpose of the discriminant is to find the zeroes, but even more importantly, it tells us how many zeroes there are. This is because:
• Only positive numbers have two square roots.
• Zero has just one square root, namely zero.
• Negative numbers have no square roots.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation of the real-root interpretation; no practice task.

entries.description:
The Zeroes (x-intercepts) of the quadratic y = ax² + bx + c
Always find the discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac before finding the zeroes.
• If Δ > 0, there are two zeroes, x = (−b + √Δ)/(2a) and x = (−b − √Δ)/(2a).
• If Δ = 0, there is just one double zero, x = −b/(2a).
  ▹ In this situation, the quadratic is a perfect square,
  ▹ and the x-axis is tangent to the graph.
• If Δ < 0, there are no zeroes.

entries.description:
The discriminant tells us whether the zeroes are rational or irrational
Suppose now that all three coefficients of y = ax² + bx + c are rational numbers. Then because we need to take the square root of Δ, the zeroes will also be rational numbers if Δ is a square. But if Δ is not a square and Δ > 0, the zeroes will involve a surd and be irrational.
